As the barrier to "vibecoding" continues to drop, the number of new apps appearing on the App Store has surged — with new submissions doubling in the first half of 2026 — yet downloads grew by just 2%. Details below.

New submissions surge, but downloads fail to keep pace

A report published today by The New York Times, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, notes that the number of new apps submitted to the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, while downloads grew by only 2%:

The New York Times piece also profiles two developers who have been steadily releasing "vibecoded" apps on the App Store — Marco Pérez, who plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to work on apps full-time, and David Svensson, who has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months and treats "vibecoding" more as a hobby than a business.

Excerpted from the report:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never built a mobile app before. He spent five weeks over the winter working with "vibecoding" AI tools to build a prototype, followed by two weeks of preparation to get it onto the App Store. His app, called InfoDrizzle, has performed reasonably well, recording around 1,300 downloads so far and generating roughly US$500 in profit. His second app has done even better. In May, he spent only about a week building Stampa — a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps. Stampa has since been downloaded 20,000 times, bringing in around US$3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian, responding to The New York Times, also addressed another issue stemming from this submission boom — earlier reports indicated that the App Store review process has come under strain as a result.

Ajemian said "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," adding that Apple is "thrilled to see a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and ship apps faster than ever before."

He also stressed that, regardless of whether an app is built using "vibecoding," "all apps must meet the same stringent standards of quality, privacy and safety that users have come to trust."
